FOR INDEPENDENT PROPANE (LP GAS) DELIVERY ROUTE OPERATORS

Gallons delivered isn't profit. Margin per customer is.

A customer who "took 850 gallons this year" can still be barely worth the trip once the small-fill trips, tank rental, and hazmat compliance cost come out of the retail/wholesale spread. This free calculator finds real annual and monthly profit for one customer, then rolls your whole route up into a number you can check against your income goal.

Wondering whether a low-volume or small-fill customer is still worth keeping on the route? See is a small propane customer worth keeping? for a worked example of a minimum-delivery fee turning a losing account profitable. Tracking margins in a spreadsheet today instead? See this calculator vs. a spreadsheet.

Private by default

Everything on this page runs in your browser and nothing is ever uploaded. Your customer inputs (annual gallons, fill size, price spread, minimum-delivery terms, drive time and mileage, tank rental and hazmat cost) and your target monthly income are saved locally on this device so you don't retype them next time — Reset to defaults clears them, and Copy shareable link puts them in a URL fragment your browser never sends anywhere. Your customer rows in the route table are a different promise: they are never saved anywhere, and closing or refreshing the tab clears them. There is no account. We count only anonymous local feature events (customer-priced, route-check, link-copied, reset) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no customers, prices, or gallon counts are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Common questions

Why does average fill size matter as much as annual gallons?

Because your annual gallon volume tells you the fuel margin, but the average fill size decides how many separate truck trips it takes to deliver that volume. A customer who takes the same annual gallons in fewer, larger fills costs you far less in drive time and mileage than one who takes it in many small top-offs — and a small enough average fill can also trigger a minimum-delivery fee, if you charge one.

Why is tank rental a fixed cost instead of something charged per gallon?

Because that is how most company-owned tank placements actually work — you carry the tank's lease or amortized cost every month whether the customer takes one delivery a year or four. This calculator applies it as a flat monthly cost so it shows up next to the fuel margin it makes possible, rather than being folded invisibly into the price per gallon.

Does this tool tell me how much propane a tank needs or when a customer will run out?

No. This calculator only prices the route economics of a delivery you have already scheduled, from numbers you supply. It does not size a tank, forecast degree-day usage, determine a safe fill level, or replace your own licensed propane supplier's delivery-scheduling and safety judgment.

Does anything about my customers or pricing get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and the customer list you type into the route section is never saved anywhere — it exists only in the page while it is open. The customer inputs above and the target monthly income setting are different: those are saved locally on this device, so you don't retype them, and a shareable link can carry them to another device. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

is-a-small-propane-customer-worth-keepin.text:
← Propane delivery route margin calculator

Is a small propane customer worth keeping?

A low-volume account's annual gallon count does not say whether the trip to fill their tank turns a profit. That number does not show the mileage, your own drive and stop-time labor, the tank rental you carry every month whether they take one delivery or four, or whether the fill is small enough that a minimum-delivery fee should apply. Two customers with the same "gallons a year" figure can land on opposite sides of zero once those come out.

Open the free route margin calculator

What an annual-gallon count hides

Fill size, not just volume. The same annual gallons split into many small top-offs means more separate truck trips than the same volume taken in fewer, larger fills — and each trip carries its own mileage and labor cost no matter how few gallons go into the tank.

Tank rental, whether or not the truck rolls. If you own the tank at the customer's property, the lease or amortized cost runs every month regardless of delivery frequency — it is the line most likely to get folded invisibly into "the price per gallon" instead of counted on its own.

Hazmat compliance cost. Your DOT hazmat endorsement, vehicle, and cargo-insurance cost has to be allocated across your customer base somehow, and a low-volume account carries the same share as a high-volume one.

The minimum-delivery fee, if you charge one. Dispatching a truck costs roughly the same whether the fill is 300 gallons or 70 — a minimum-delivery fee on small fills is how many dealers recover that fixed dispatch cost instead of eating it on every small stop.

Worked example

A customer takes 220 gallons a year in small 70-gallon fills, at a $2.49 retail price against a $1.55 wholesale cost, over an 18-mile round trip at $0.95/mile, 20 minutes on-site plus 22 minutes round-trip drive at a $28/hour target rate, a $5/month tank rental, and a $3.50/month hazmat compliance allocation. First with no minimum-delivery fee charged, even though the 70-gallon fill is below a 100-gallon minimum-delivery threshold:

FigureNo minimum feeWith a $45 minimum fee
Deliveries per year3.14 (220 ÷ 70)
Fuel margin revenue$206.80 (220 × $0.94)
Minimum-delivery fee revenue$0.00 (not charged)$141.43 (3.14 × $45)
Annual revenue$206.80$348.23
Mileage$53.74 (18 mi × $0.95 × 3.14 trips)
Your labor$61.60 (2.2 hrs/yr at $28/hr)
Tank rental + hazmat$102.00 ($60 + $42/yr)
Total annual cost$217.34
Net profit (annual)−$10.54$130.89
Net profit (monthly)−$0.88$10.91
Profit margin−5.1%37.6%
Profit per gallon−$0.05$0.59

Same customer, same 220 gallons, same 18-mile trip — a small-fill account that quietly loses money every year turns into real profit once a $45 minimum-delivery fee recovers the fixed cost of the dispatch. The fee did not change what the customer uses; it changed who pays for the trip a small fill still requires.

Common questions

How do I know if a small propane customer is actually worth keeping on the route?

Subtract mileage, your own drive and stop-time labor, tank rental, and hazmat compliance cost from the fuel margin (retail minus wholesale price times annual gallons) plus any minimum-delivery fee the fill size triggers. A 220-gallon-a-year customer taking small 70-gallon fills can lose about $10.54 a year with no minimum fee charged, and turn into a $130.89 annual profit once a $45 minimum-delivery fee is added — same customer, same gallons, same drive.

Why does a small average fill size cost so much more than the fuel margin alone suggests?

Because the same annual gallons split into smaller fills means more separate truck trips — each carrying its own mileage and drive/stop-time labor cost regardless of how few gallons go into the tank that visit. A customer who could take the same annual volume in half as many fills costs you roughly half the trips for the identical fuel margin.

Is a minimum-delivery fee the only way to fix a losing small-fill customer?

It is the most direct lever, because it recovers the fixed cost of dispatching a truck regardless of fill size, but it is not the only one. Widening the retail/wholesale spread for that customer, batching their delivery with a neighboring stop to cut mileage, or asking them to accept a larger tank and fewer, bigger fills can each move the number — a minimum fee is simply the one that does not depend on the customer changing anything.

Does this calculator decide whether it is safe to space out a customer's deliveries?

No. It only prices the route economics of deliveries you have already scheduled, from numbers you supply. Whether a customer's tank can safely go longer between fills, and how much propane it needs, are supply and safety questions for your own licensed judgment — this tool never touches them.

vs-tracking-propane-delivery-margin-in-a.text:
← Propane delivery route margin calculator

This calculator vs. tracking propane delivery margin in a spreadsheet

Names no specific product or company — this compares a free calculator against the generic method most independent propane dealers already use: a personal or shared spreadsheet with a margin formula typed in once and copied down for every customer.

QuestionSpreadsheet formulaThis calculator
Minimum-delivery fee thresholdA manual IF formula per row, easy to leave off a new customer or get backwards (charged when it should not be, or the reverse)Applies the threshold the same way on every customer, and states plainly whether it triggered
Deliveries per year from fill sizeAn extra column you have to add and keep dividing correctly as fill size changesComputed automatically from annual gallons ÷ average fill size
Fixed monthly cost per customerOften folded invisibly into "the price per gallon" instead of tracked on its ownTank rental and hazmat compliance cost are separate line items, every time
Whole-route income checkA second sheet or a manual sum, often not kept in sync with the per-customer tabBuilt in — enter each customer's monthly profit and see the route total against your income goal
History across customers and seasonsIts actual strength — a running log with address, tank ownership, and delivery historyPrices one customer at a time; does not replace a customer log
Shareable single scenarioRequires sending the whole file or a screenshotOne link, via "Copy shareable link," with no file attached

Neither tool determines your retail price, your wholesale cost, or how much propane a tank needs — both are arithmetic on numbers you already have, and both are only as accurate as the figures you type in.

Common questions

Why not just track propane customer margins in a spreadsheet?

Plenty of small dealers do, and a spreadsheet is a fine tool for tracking a customer list over a season. The failure mode is not the spreadsheet itself — it is the minimum-delivery-fee threshold, which is a conditional (does this fill size trigger the fee, yes or no) that a copied-down formula has to re-implement correctly for every row, and easy to get wrong once for a new customer with an unusual fill size. A calculator that re-evaluates the condition on every input avoids that particular drift; a spreadsheet formula copied down a column does not check itself.

Does this calculator replace my customer spreadsheet?

Not necessarily. This tool prices one customer at a time and does not save a running list across sessions the way a spreadsheet's rows do. Many small dealers use both: this calculator to get one customer's arithmetic right, including the minimum-delivery-fee edge case, and their own spreadsheet to log the result alongside address, tank ownership, and delivery history for every customer over a season.
